sections.guidingQuestion: Which molecule directly uses a DNA template to synthesize a transcript?
sections.explanation:
Transcription synthesizes RNA using one DNA strand as a template. RNA polymerase locally separates the DNA strands, selects complementary RNA nucleotides and joins them by phosphodiester bonds.

The DNA strands rejoin behind RNA polymerase. The product is an RNA transcript of a selected region, not a second DNA molecule. The same gene can be transcribed repeatedly without its DNA sequence being consumed.

sections.guidingQuestion: Which 5′→3′ RNA sequence is transcribed from template 3′-TAC-5′?
sections.explanation:
During transcription, DNA A pairs with RNA U, T with A, C with G and G with C. Hydrogen bonds allow incoming RNA nucleotides to pair with the template; RNA polymerase forms the covalent bonds joining the new RNA strand.

RNA is complementary to the DNA template. It resembles the coding DNA strand, with U replacing T. For aligned strands, template DNA 3′-TAC CGA ATT-5′ corresponds to RNA 5′-AUG GCU UAA-3′ and coding DNA 5′-ATG GCT TAA-3′. These labels make the example unambiguous; synthesis directionality is developed in D1.2.12 (HL).

sections.guidingQuestion: Why can a non-dividing neuron repeatedly transcribe one gene?
sections.explanation:
RNA polymerase reads the DNA base sequence without consuming it or turning it into RNA. The locally separated strands rejoin after transcription, leaving the original sequence available to be read again.

Non-dividing somatic cells, such as many neurons, need to conserve their DNA sequences throughout their lives while making fresh RNA and proteins. Repeated transcription allows this. Stability does not mean DNA can never be damaged or mutated.

sections.guidingQuestion: Which is a major stage at which a cell regulates whether a gene is expressed?
sections.explanation:
Not all genes in a cell are expressed at any given time. Transcription is the first stage of gene expression and a key point at which a gene can be switched on or off. If a protein-coding gene is not transcribed, no new mRNA from it is supplied for translation.

Cells with essentially the same genes can produce different proteins because they transcribe different genes. For example, pancreatic beta cells transcribe the insulin gene much more actively than most other cells. This changes cell function without requiring a change in the gene’s DNA sequence.

sections.guidingQuestion: What is the direct product of translating an mRNA coding region?
sections.explanation:
Translation uses the base sequence of mRNA to determine the amino-acid sequence of a polypeptide. A ribosome reads successive three-base codons and joins the corresponding amino acids by peptide bonds.

tRNAs deliver amino acids to the ribosome; codons do not become amino acids or supply their atoms. The resulting chain may need folding or modification to function as a protein. Translation makes a polypeptide, whereas transcription makes RNA.

sections.guidingQuestion: Which anticodon pairs with mRNA codon 5′-AUG-3′?
sections.explanation:
A codon is a triplet of bases on mRNA; an anticodon is a complementary triplet on tRNA. Hydrogen bonding between them helps select the tRNA carrying the amino acid specified by the codon. A tRNA must carry the appropriate amino acid before its anticodon pairs with an mRNA codon; the amino-acid attachment site and the anticodon are different parts of the molecule.

In an aligned example, mRNA 5′-AUG-3′ pairs with anticodon 3′-UAC-5′. Use AUG, not the anticodon, in an mRNA codon table: AUG specifies methionine. Anticodons pair with mRNA; they are not copied into the polypeptide.

sections.guidingQuestion: Why is a triplet code necessary to encode 20 standard amino acids?
sections.explanation:
Four RNA bases give only 4² = 16 two-base combinations, too few for 20 standard amino acids. Three-base codons give 4³ = 64 combinations, enough for amino acids and stop signals.

The code is degenerate: several codons can specify the same amino acid, although each ordinary codon has a definite meaning. It is nearly universal across life, supporting common ancestry; some organisms and organelles use variant codes. Degeneracy can make a base substitution synonymous, leaving the amino acid unchanged.

sections.explanation:

sections.guidingQuestion: What is removed when proinsulin is converted to mature insulin?
sections.explanation:
Many new polypeptides need folding, cleavage, covalent modification or association with other chains before functioning. These are changes to proteins, unlike splicing, which processes RNA.

First, the signal peptide is removed from preproinsulin in the secretory pathway, producing proinsulin. Proinsulin folds and forms disulfide bonds. Second, removal of the connecting C-peptide produces mature insulin, whose A and B chains remain linked by disulfide bonds. The ribosome does not directly make free mature two-chain insulin.

sections.guidingQuestion: What type of macromolecule is principally degraded by a proteasome?
sections.explanation:
Maintaining a functional proteome requires continual protein synthesis and breakdown. Damaged, misfolded or unneeded proteins must be removed rather than allowed to accumulate.

Proteasomes degrade selected proteins into short peptides, which can be further broken down to reusable amino acids. This recovers building materials for new protein synthesis. Degrading a protein does not delete its DNA gene, and proteasomes are not the only protein-degradation system.
